diagnostic_evidence.quote: To ensure the injectivity of the encoder approximated by a neural network, each layer must be injective, condition which is satisfied when $n_\ell \geq n_{\ell-1}$ for all hidden layers, so $n_\ell \geq n_\text{in}$ for $\ell = 1,\ldots,L-1$.

issues.failure_explanation: The theorem asserts that having hidden layer widths $n_\ell \geq n_\text{in}$ is sufficient to guarantee injectivity of the encoder network $\Psi': \mathbb{R}^N \to \mathbb{R}^n$. The proof claims that each hidden layer is injective whenever $n_\ell \geq n_{\ell-1}$, and that this ensures injectivity of the encoder. This reasoning fails for two reasons: first, standard activation functions such as ReLU map non-positive inputs to zero and are non-injective regardless of layer widths, and weight matrices with $n_\ell \geq n_{\ell-1}$ need not be full-rank; second, the output layer maps from $n_{L-1} \geq N$ to $n < N$, which cannot be injective on its domain. A condition on hidden layer widths alone cannot guarantee injectivity of a dimension-reducing neural network.

failure_location.quote: A sufficient condition for the width to ensure injectivity of the encoder is $n_\ell \geq n_\text{in}$, for $\ell = 1,\ldots, L-1$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Weaken Theorem 2 to state the existence of an encoder embedding based on topological embedding theorems and universal approximation of embeddings, rather than claiming that an arbitrary or trained network with hidden widths $n_\ell \geq n_\text{in}$ is automatically injective.
issues.overall_effect: The architectural guarantee that the representation error vanishes ($\Varepsilon_1 = 0$) solely by enforcing $n_\ell \geq n_\text{in}$ is unsupported.
issues.title: Layer width condition does not ensure injectivity of the encoder
issues.why_classification: The claim can be repaired by replacing the layer-by-layer injectivity assertion with an existence statement for embedding networks, preserving the overall reduction methodology without developing a new global proof framework.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: thus $B_r((t,\mu))\to U$ is a local homeomorphism. We conclude that $U$ is locally Euclidean, so $\{u_N(t;\mu)\}_{t\in[0,T], \mu \in \mathcal{P}}$ is a $a$-manifold, that we denote by $\mathcal{M}$.

issues.failure_explanation: The theorem concludes that the image $\{u_N(t; \mu)\}$ is an $a$-manifold assuming only local injectivity of $(t, \mu) \mapsto u_N(t; \mu)$. A continuous, locally injective map from a compact domain is an immersion, not necessarily an embedding. If the map is not globally injective—such as when a periodic orbit closes or trajectories for different parameter values cross—the image contains self-intersections. In the subspace topology, neighborhoods of self-intersection points are homeomorphic to intersecting branches rather than Euclidean balls, violating the definition of a manifold. Additionally, $[0, T] \times \mathcal{P}$ has boundaries and corners, so the image can at best be a manifold with boundary.

failure_location.quote: and the map $B_r((t^*,\mu^*)) \ni (t, \mu) \to u_N$ is injective $\forall (t^*, \mu^*) \in [0,T]\times\mathcal{P}$, with $r$ small enough. Then, the set $\{u_N(t;\mu)\}_{t\in[0,T], \mu \in \mathcal{P}}$ is a $a$-manifold.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Add the hypothesis that the parameter-and-time-to-solution map $(t, \mu) \mapsto u_N(t; \mu)$ is globally injective (or consider the augmented solution set as noted in Observation 2) and formulate the result for an $a$-manifold with boundary.
issues.overall_effect: Theorem 3 and the subsequent application of the Menger-Nöbeling embedding theorem in Theorem 4 are mathematically invalid unless global injectivity and boundary behavior are properly accounted for.
issues.title: Local injectivity does not guarantee that the solution set is a topological manifold
issues.why_classification: Adding global injectivity is a standard local hypothesis fix that directly validates the embedding argument of Theorem 3 and preserves Theorem 4 without altering any subsequent results.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Due to the specific assumptions made in the construction of the decoder, the projection sets some eigenvalues to zero while leaving the others unchanged. Therefore, the eigenvalues $\neq 0$ are those of $\Lambda$, so the bound on the timestep of the \node\ is, in the worst scenario, the same as that of the \Node.

issues.failure_explanation: In Section 5.4 (Step 2, Linear encoder, linear decoder), the text asserts that the decoder can be constructed as $J_\Psi = (J_{\Psi'}^\top J_{\Psi'})^{-1}J_{\Psi'}^\top$. Because $J_{\Psi'} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times N}$ with $n < N$, the matrix $J_{\Psi'}^\top J_{\Psi'}$ is $N \times N$ of rank at most $n$, making it singular and non-invertible. Furthermore, the text claims that for the projection $P = J_\Psi J_{\Psi'}$, the non-zero eigenvalues of $P \Lambda$ are equal to the eigenvalues of $\Lambda$. This is mathematically false: an orthogonal projection of a matrix onto a subspace does not preserve its eigenvalues (they become Ritz values). In fact, compressing a Hurwitz matrix $\Lambda$ onto a subspace can produce eigenvalues with positive real parts, so the stability limit of Forward Euler for the reduced system is not generally bounded by that of the full system.

failure_location.quote: This property can be achieved, for example, constructing the decoder as $J_\Psi = (J_{\Psi'}^\top J_{\Psi'})^{-1}J_{\Psi'}^\top$

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Withdraw the claim of eigenvalue preservation for generic projections, correct the pseudoinverse formulation to $(J_{\Psi'} J_{\Psi'}^\top)^{-1}$ (or state that the decoder is a right inverse), and restrict the stability guarantee to invariant subspaces of $\Lambda$ or symmetric negative definite matrices where Rayleigh quotients apply.
issues.overall_effect: The guarantee that the Forward Euler stability limit of the reduced linear model is bounded by that of the full-order system is false and unsupported as stated.
issues.title: Singular matrix inversion and false preservation of eigenvalues under projection
issues.why_classification: The claim is materially false and requires withdrawing or restricting the unconditional A-stability preservation guarantee for linear reductions, but the remainder of the reduction framework remains viable.
